summary: Italian questions need no do and no special word order: a statement becomes a question by intonation alone. The work is in the question word: picking it (che cosa, chi, quale, quanto), making it agree where it can, and putting any preposition in front of it. The idea that makes it click: the preposition never stays at the end, so with whom, not who ... with.

subs.label: che cosa, cosa, che and chi
subs.focus: What is che cosa, cosa or che, all three correct and interchangeable before a verb (che cosa fai, cosa fai, che fai); who is chi, for one person or several. When chi is the subject the verb is third person singular (chi viene stasera, chi ha chiamato); with essere and a plural noun it is chi sono (chi sono quei ragazzi). Typical errors: cosa for a person or chi for a thing (Chi è questo? about an object), a plural verb after subject chi (chi vengono alla festa), che used for who (Che ha telefonato?). Do not make the learner choose between che cosa, cosa and che: never use one of them as a wrong option against another.

subs.label: qual è il tuo numero, che lavoro fai
subs.focus: English what + is + noun asking for one answer out of the possible ones (name, number, address, capital, problem) is qual è / quali sono, not che cosa è: qual è il tuo numero, qual è il problema, quali sono i tuoi programmi. Che cos'è asks for a definition or what an unknown thing is (che cos'è questo). Before a noun, what kind of is che (che lavoro fai, che musica ascolti) and which of a set is quale / quali (quale vino preferisci, quali scarpe metti). Spelling: qual è with no apostrophe; quale has only one plural, quali, for both genders. Typical errors: che cosa è il tuo indirizzo, cosa è il tuo nome, qual'è, quale with a plural noun (quale libri), quala or quale for quali. Where both che and quale are natural before a noun (che film / quale film vuoi vedere), do not use one as the wrong option against the other.

subs.label: quanto, quanta, quanti, quante
subs.focus: Before a noun quanto agrees with it in gender and number: quanto tempo, quanta pasta, quanti anni, quante persone. Alone with a verb it is an adverb and stays quanto, whatever the subject: quanto costa, quanto costano queste scarpe, quanto dura il film. When the noun is understood it still agrees (quanti ne vuoi, quante siete). Typical errors: quanto left unchanged before a noun (quanto persone, quanto anni hai), wrong gender (quanti volte, quanto acqua), agreement with the subject when it is an adverb (quanti costano questi), and di inserted after it (quanti di fratelli hai).

subs.label: dove, come, quando, perché, come mai
subs.focus: Dove, come, quando and perché never change form; dove and come normally lose the vowel before è and era (dov'è, com'è, dov'era). Perché is both why in the question and because in the answer; come mai is a softer, more surprised why (how come). Come also asks for a description (com'è il tuo nuovo capo) and for a name (come ti chiami). Typical errors: quando for dove and the reverse, cosa ti chiami for come ti chiami, come è written out where com'è is normal, a separate word for because (Perché sei stanco? - Per sono...), come for come mai or for perché, perchè or perche for perché.

subs.label: di dove sei, con chi esci, a che ora
subs.focus: A preposition that belongs to the question word goes immediately in front of it and never at the end of the sentence: di dove sei, da dove vieni, con chi esci, a chi scrivi, per chi è, di chi è questa borsa (whose), a che ora parte, a che cosa pensi, di che cosa parlate, in quale città abiti, da quanto tempo, fino a quando. The preposition is the one the verb or expression takes in a statement (penso a, parlo di, esco con). Typical errors: stranding (Chi esci con?, Dove sei di?), dropping it (Che ora parte il treno?, Chi è questa borsa? for whose, Dove vieni? for where do you come from), the wrong one (A dove sei?, Di chi pensi? for a chi pensi), and putting it after the question word (chi con esci).

subs.label: dove abita Maria? and questions with no do
subs.focus: A yes or no question has the word order of a statement and only the intonation or the question mark changes: Parli italiano?, Maria lavora domani?. There is no helping verb like do. After a question word the verb comes straight after it and a noun subject follows the verb or goes to the very front or end: Dove abita Maria?, Quanto costa questo?, Maria dove abita?. Perché and come mai are the main exceptions: the subject can stay before the verb (Perché Luca non viene?). Subject pronouns are normally left out. Typical errors: subject between question word and verb (Dove Maria abita?, Che cosa tuo fratello studia?, Quando il treno parte?), fare added as do (Fai parli italiano?, Dove fai abiti?). In ordering items accept every natural order, including the subject at the front.

subs.label: non so dove abita, mi chiedo se viene
subs.focus: After sapere, chiedere, chiedersi, dire, capire, ricordare and similar verbs the question keeps its question word, with the preposition still in front, and no question mark unless the main clause is itself a question: non so dove abita, dimmi con chi esci, non ricordo a che ora parte. A yes or no question is introduced by se (whether, if): non so se viene, mi chiedo se è aperto. What is che cosa or cosa (non so cosa vuole). Only the indicative is used here; the subjunctive is another topic. Typical errors: che for se (non so che viene domani for whether), se left out (non so viene), se added before a question word (non so se dove abita), stranded preposition (non so chi esce con). Non so quello che vuole is correct Italian and must not be used as a wrong option.

subs.label: vero? and no? at the end
subs.focus: English tags (isn't it, don't you, did he) are all one fixed word in Italian, added after a comma: vero? after an affirmative or a negative statement, no? mainly after an affirmative one; giusto? and non è vero? also exist. The verb is not repeated. Typical errors: repeating the verb as in English (Sei italiano, non sei?, Parli inglese, non fai?), sì? used as a general tag, and no? placed at the front. Do not use non è vero? as a wrong option against vero?: both are correct.

rules.rule: What is che cosa, cosa or che: all three are correct and mean the same before a verb. Who is chi, and it does not change for number or gender.
rules.pattern: che cosa / cosa / che + verb | chi + verb

examples.tl: Che cosa fai questo fine settimana?
examples.en: What are you doing this weekend?
What do you want to eat tonight?

examples.tl: Chi è quella signora con il cappello?
examples.en: Who is that lady with the hat?

examples.tl: Chi hai visto ieri alla festa?
examples.en: Who did you see at the party yesterday?

rules.note: Before è, cosa and che cosa usually shorten: cos'è, che cos'è. Che alone before a verb (Che fai?) is informal but very common.

rules.rule: When chi is the subject, the verb is third person singular even if you expect several people. With essere followed by a plural noun or pronoun, the verb agrees with that: chi sono.
rules.pattern: chi + verb in 3rd singular | chi sono + plural noun

examples.tl: Chi viene al cinema con noi?
examples.en: Who is coming to the cinema with us?

examples.tl: Chi ha preso le mie chiavi?
examples.en: Who took my keys?

examples.tl: Chi sono quei ragazzi davanti alla scuola?
examples.en: Who are those boys in front of the school?

rules.rule: What is + noun, when the answer picks one out of the possible ones (a name, a number, an address, a capital), is qual è, plural quali sono. Che cos'è asks what an unknown thing is or asks for a definition.
rules.pattern: qual è + singular noun | quali sono + plural noun | che cos'è + thing to explain

examples.tl: Qual è il tuo numero di telefono?
examples.en: What is your phone number?

examples.tl: Qual è la capitale della Svizzera?
examples.en: What is the capital of Switzerland?

examples.tl: Quali sono i tuoi programmi per l'estate?
examples.en: What are your plans for the summer?
What is this noise?

rules.note: Qual è is written with no apostrophe. Quale has one plural for both genders: quali.

rules.rule: Before a noun, che asks what or what kind of, and quale / quali asks which one of a set. Quale agrees in number with the noun. In many sentences both are possible.
rules.pattern: che + noun | quale + singular noun, quali + plural noun

examples.en: What does your sister do for a living?
What music do you usually listen to?

examples.tl: Quale vino preferisci, il rosso o il bianco?
examples.en: Which wine do you prefer, the red or the white?

examples.tl: Quali scarpe metti per il matrimonio?
examples.en: Which shoes are you wearing to the wedding?

rules.note: Che cosa and cosa are never put before a noun: che lavoro fai, not che cosa lavoro fai.

rules.rule: Before a noun, quanto agrees with it like an adjective. With a verb and no noun it is an adverb and stays quanto, even when the subject is plural.
rules.pattern: quanto + masc. sing. | quanta + fem. sing. | quanti + masc. pl. | quante + fem. pl. | quanto + verb

examples.en: How old is your son?
How many people are coming to dinner?
How much pasta should I cook?
How much do these shoes cost?

rules.note: No di after it: quanti fratelli hai, not quanti di fratelli. When the noun is left out but understood, quanto still agrees with it: Quante ne vuoi? (of le mele).

rules.rule: Dove (where), come (how), quando (when) and perché (why) never change form. Before è, dove and come normally become dov'è and com'è. Come also asks what something is like and what someone is called.
rules.pattern: dove / come / quando / perché + verb | dov'è, com'è

examples.en: Where is the bus stop?
When are you coming back from your holiday?
What is your new flat like?
What is your brother called?

rules.rule: Perché is why in the question and because in the answer: one word for both. Come mai also asks why, in a softer way that shows surprise, like how come.

examples.en: Why don't you eat meat?

examples.tl: Non la mangio perché sono vegetariana.
examples.en: I don't eat it because I am a vegetarian.

examples.tl: Come mai sei già a casa?
examples.en: How come you are already home?

rules.note: Perché is written with an acute accent: é, not è.

rules.rule: A preposition that goes with the question word stands directly in front of it. It never stays at the end of the sentence as in English, and it is never dropped. Use the preposition the verb takes in a statement: esco con Anna gives con chi esci.
rules.pattern: preposition + chi / che cosa / dove / quale + noun / che + noun / quanto + noun

examples.en: Who are you going out with tonight?
Where are you from?

examples.tl: A che ora parte il treno per Napoli?
examples.en: What time does the train to Naples leave?
What are you thinking about?

rules.note: Di dove sei asks for your home town or country (with essere); da dove vieni asks where you are coming from (with venire, arrivare).

rules.rule: Whose is di chi, followed by essere. For whom is per chi, to whom is a chi, and how long or since when starts with da: da quanto tempo.
rules.pattern: di chi è / sono + noun | per chi | a chi | in quale + noun | da quanto tempo

examples.en: Whose bag is this?
Who are these flowers for?

examples.tl: In quale città abitano i tuoi genitori?
examples.en: Which city do your parents live in?
How long have you been studying Italian?

rules.rule: A yes or no question is a statement said with rising intonation: the words stay in the same order and there is no helping verb like do. After a question word the verb comes straight after it, and a noun subject goes after the verb or at the very front. After perché and come mai the subject can also stay before the verb.
rules.pattern: statement + ? | question word + verb + subject | subject, question word + verb | perché + subject + verb

examples.en: Does your brother speak English?
Where does Maria live now?
How much does this ticket cost?

examples.tl: Perché Luca non risponde al telefono?
examples.en: Why isn't Luca answering the phone?

rules.note: Maria dove abita? is also natural: the subject is named first as the topic. What does not work is the subject between the question word and the verb: Dove Maria abita?

rules.rule: A question inside another sentence keeps its question word, with any preposition still in front of it. A yes or no question is introduced by se, which covers both whether and if.
rules.pattern: non so / dimmi / mi chiedo + question word ... | non so / mi chiedo + se ...

examples.tl: Non so dove abita il nuovo collega.
examples.en: I don't know where the new colleague lives.

examples.tl: Mi chiedo se il museo è aperto oggi.
examples.en: I wonder whether the museum is open today.

examples.tl: Dimmi con chi vai in vacanza.
examples.en: Tell me who you are going on holiday with.

examples.tl: Sai a che ora chiude la farmacia?
examples.en: Do you know what time the chemist's closes?

rules.note: The question mark appears only when the main clause is a question (Sai ...?). After non so and mi chiedo careful speakers often use the subjunctive, but the indicative shown here is normal in everyday Italian.

rules.rule: To ask for confirmation, add vero? after a comma: it works after affirmative and negative statements alike. No? does the same job, mainly after affirmative statements. The verb is not repeated as in English.

examples.en: You are from Milan, aren't you?

examples.tl: Il film comincia alle nove, no?
examples.en: The film starts at nine, doesn't it?
You haven't eaten yet, have you?

right.en: Who are you going out with tonight?

contrasts.why: An Italian preposition cannot be left at the end of the sentence. It moves to the front with its question word: con chi.

right.tl: A che ora comincia la lezione?
right.en: What time does the lesson start?

contrasts.why: English can drop at, but Italian cannot drop a: the lesson starts alle nove, so the question is a che ora.
Whose is di chi, literally of whom. Chi è alone asks who a person is.

contrasts.wrong: Che cosa è il tuo indirizzo?
contrasts.why: The answer picks one address out of all possible ones, so Italian asks qual è. Che cos'è would ask for a definition of the thing.

contrasts.wrong: Quanto persone lavorano in questo ufficio?

right.tl: Quante persone lavorano in questo ufficio?
right.en: How many people work in this office?

contrasts.why: Before a noun quanto agrees with it: persone is feminine plural, so quante.

right.en: How much do these trousers cost?

contrasts.why: Here quanto goes with the verb costano, not with a noun, so it is an adverb and does not change. Only the verb is plural.
After dove the verb comes first and the noun subject follows it. Tua sorella dove lavora? is also possible, but the subject cannot stand between dove and the verb.

contrasts.wrong: Chi vengono alla riunione di domani?

right.tl: Chi viene alla riunione di domani?
right.en: Who is coming to tomorrow's meeting?

contrasts.why: Chi as subject takes a singular verb, even when the answer will be several people.

contrasts.wrong: Non so che Paolo viene alla festa o no.

right.tl: Non so se Paolo viene alla festa o no.
right.en: I don't know whether Paolo is coming to the party or not.

contrasts.why: Whether and if in an indirect yes or no question are se. Che means that and cannot introduce a question.
Italian has no helping verb like do and does not repeat the verb in a tag. One fixed word does the job: vero? or no?.

cheat: what = che cosa / cosa / che (all fine); who = chi, with a singular verb when it is the subject: chi viene?
what is your name, number, address: qual è (no apostrophe), quali sono; che cos'è only asks what a thing is.
che + noun = what, what kind of (che lavoro fai); quale / quali + noun = which one of a set.
quanto agrees before a noun (quanti anni, quante persone) and stays quanto with a verb (quanto costano).
Preposition first, never last and never dropped: con chi, di dove, a che ora, di chi è, da quanto tempo.
No do: Parli italiano? Question word + verb + subject: Dove abita Maria? Perché is both why and because.
Inside a sentence: non so dove abita, non so se viene. Tag: ..., vero? or ..., no?
